PMGT1711 Week 07

PMGT1711 Week 7 - Soft Systems Methodology and Multimethodology in Series

Understanding Unstructured Project Situations

Soft Systems Methodology (SSM) is an organised process of inquiry for situations in which people disagree about what the problem is, what the project should achieve, or what improvement means. An unstructured problem is ambiguous, unfamiliar or incompletely specified and requires judgement rather than a single predetermined answer. People interpret problems and possible solutions through different assumptions, relationships and values. The analyst also participates in this interpretation rather than standing completely outside it.

Hard systems thinking generally starts with sufficiently defined objectives and seeks a workable or optimised means of achieving them. Soft systems thinking explores the objectives themselves through participation, interpretation and learning. Neither approach is universally superior: the method should fit the situation. SSM is particularly useful in early project definition, before detailed planning assumes that the direction is settled.

A project can involve several forms of complexity:

Type

Main concern

Structural

Numerous interconnected elements and dependencies

Technical

Innovation and uncertainty about how to achieve an outcome

Directional

Unclear or contested purposes and objectives

Temporal

Environmental conditions changing over time

Relational

Interdependent people, coordination, trust and power

Front-ending means using problem-structuring methods before conventional project planning and delivery. It clarifies what should be done before decomposing the work into tasks.

Models as Learning Devices

An SSM model is a device for learning about a situation, not an exact replica of reality or an instruction to implement a particular design. Different models can represent different purposeful interpretations of the same situation.

The aim is to improve a continuing problem situation, rather than assume that a neatly bounded problem can be permanently solved. Hierarchy, communication, control and emergence can all inform inquiry. Emergence means that interactions generate patterns not adequately understood by examining the participants separately.

Rich Pictures

A rich picture is a free-form representation using images, symbols, arrows and short labels. It expresses people, relationships, processes, feelings, tensions and value judgements. Its purpose is to retain the messiness that a tidy process diagram may conceal; artistic quality is unimportant.

Useful elements include:

• Participants and groups, including people whose perspectives are absent.

• Relationships, alliances, disagreements and power differences.

• Flows of money, information, approvals and feedback.

• System boundaries and relationships between wider systems and smaller subsystems.

• Emotions such as pride, confusion, resistance or frustration.

Root Definitions and P-Q-R

A root definition states what a purposeful activity system does from a particular perspective. A useful form is:

A system to do P, by Q, in order to contribute to R.

Symbol

Meaning

Function

P

What is done

Identifies the transformation or purposeful activity

Q

How it is done

Identifies the means or process

R

Why it is done

Identifies the purpose that makes the activity worthwhile

The stated purpose may reveal a worldview, but a purpose statement and the complete worldview are not automatically identical.

CATWOE

CATWOE is a mnemonic for testing and developing a purposeful interpretation of a system.

Letter

Term

Meaning

C

Customers

People who benefit from, or suffer from, the transformation

A

Actors

People who carry out the transformation

T

Transformation

A change from an input state to an output state

W

Worldview

The perspective that makes this transformation meaningful

O

Owners

People with authority to stop the transformation

E

Environmental constraints

External conditions treated as given for the analysis

Worldview and transformation are central. One useful order is W, T, C, A, O, E: establish why the activity matters and what changes before identifying roles and constraints. Construct a separate CATWOE analysis for each materially different perspective.

A conceptual activity model then identifies the activities logically required by the root definition. It is built from that purposeful interpretation rather than copied from an existing organisational chart.

Evaluating Purposeful Activity: The Three Es

Criterion

Question

Efficacy

Does the transformation produce its intended immediate result?

Efficiency

How much output is obtained for the resources consumed?

Effectiveness

Does the transformation contribute to the longer-term purpose?

A basic efficiency ratio is:

Efficiency = quantity of output / quantity of resources used

The numerator measures useful output and the denominator measures a specified resource, such as staff hours or expenditure. Units must be stated: books processed per staff hour and books processed per dollar are different measures. High efficiency does not establish that the activity serves an appropriate long-term purpose. The environmental E in CATWOE is a different concept from these three evaluation criteria.

The SSM Inquiry Process

Seven Activities

Enter and investigate the unstructured situation.

Express the situation, including through rich pictures.

Develop root definitions of relevant purposeful systems.

Construct conceptual activity models.

Compare those models with the real-world situation.

Identify changes that are both desirable and feasible.

Take action to improve the situation and continue learning.

Developing definitions and models involves explicit systems thinking; investigation, comparison and action engage directly with the situation. Activities are iterative, not a compulsory one-way sequence.

A more compact formulation contains four activities:

Find out about the situation, including its cultural and political dimensions.

Build purposeful activity models.

Discuss desirable and feasible improvements and possible accommodations.

Act to improve the situation.

Two connected streams support this process. The logic-based stream develops definitions, models and reasoned comparisons. The cultural stream explores how social meanings, relationships and power affect what can actually change.

Cultural and Political Analysis

Analysis

Focus

Main concepts

One: intervention

How the inquiry is constituted

The client who initiates it, the would-be problem solver, and possible problem owners whose concerns are involved

Two: social

How social expectations shape action

Roles, norms and values that influence one another

Three: political

How interests are accommodated through power

Sources of authority, influence and control

Intervention roles describe participation in the inquiry; they are not interchangeable with CATWOE roles.

Roles are socially recognised positions, norms are expectations about behaviour, and values are judgements about what matters. In a technology organisation, values such as innovation and technical ability may interact with norms of flexibility and open communication.

Political analysis can distinguish several sources of power:

• Charismatic authority: influence associated with an individual's perceived personal qualities.

• Traditional authority: authority justified by established custom.

• Rational-legal authority: authority attached to formal rules and offices.

• Legitimate power: an accepted right to direct action.

• Coercive power: the ability to impose penalties.

• Reward power: the ability to provide benefits.

• Referent power: influence through identification, respect or affiliation.

• Expert power: influence through recognised knowledge or competence.

• Informational power: influence through access to or use of relevant information.

Desirability, Feasibility and Accommodation

A proposed change should be both systemically desirable and culturally feasible. The first condition means it is defensible through reasoning about the activity system and its wider effects. The second means it can make sense and be implemented within the actual social and political context.

Accommodation is a basis for action that participants can live with despite continuing differences. It does not require identical values or complete consensus. Models support discussion rather than command compliance.

SSM provides a flexible structure for engaging multiple perspectives. Its limitations include the possibility that powerful participants distort discussion and that coercion prevents meaningful participation. Radical change may be difficult where the inquiry cannot challenge established interests. These are contextual limitations, not proof that all situations have the same outcome. Methodological pluralism means drawing on more than one approach when necessary.

Multimethodology in Series

Multimethodology combines methods with different strengths and assumptions. In a series arrangement, exploratory problem structuring comes before more conventional problem solving. This is particularly appropriate for directional complexity: disputed objectives, hidden sponsor purposes or conflicting interpretations must be explored before detailed delivery planning becomes credible.

SSM or Strategic Options Development and Analysis (SODA) can provide this front-end inquiry. SODA structures different understandings and strategic options to support discussion. Attaching such inquiry to a conventional delivery approach is also described as grafting.

The approaches have different emphases:

Orientation

Typical emphasis

Realist or positivist

Observable facts, quantitative models, testing hypotheses and controlling performance against specified objectives

Interpretivist or social-constructivist

Negotiated meanings, qualitative participation, learning, discussion models and accommodation

These are tendencies rather than prohibitions on particular data types. Combining methods should preserve their assumptions: an exploratory discussion should not simply validate a decision already imposed.

Critical Systems Thinking argues that there is no single best methodology for all situations. Related approaches include the System of Systems Methodologies, Total Systems Intervention, combination patterns for methodologies, and deliberate intervention design.

Implementing a Series Arrangement

Select suitable methods and an experienced facilitator.

Define the desired learning and accommodation outcomes and how to evaluate them.

Explore objectives, context and workable agreements.

Allow enough time for clarification rather than rushing into implementation.

Move into delivery when the situation is sufficiently structured, carrying the findings into plans and governance.

The exploratory phase can itself be managed as a small project. Evaluation may include participants' satisfaction with the direction, but practical improvement matters more than attractive evaluation results. Different phases may require different expertise, including external facilitation.

Series works best when the clarified direction remains sufficiently stable. If environmental changes repeatedly invalidate early decisions, a parallel arrangement, in which inquiry and delivery methods operate alongside each other, may be more suitable for temporal complexity.

Cases and Applications

University Library

A librarian's root definition might be: a system to lend and manage books, by cataloguing and issuing them, so that students can access learning resources.

A student's definition might instead emphasise a quiet place to study, provided through desks and silence, so that focused study is possible. The building is the same, but the selected activity and purpose differ.

Painting a Fence

For a homeowner painting a fence by hand:

• Customers, actors and owners may all be the homeowner.

• Transformation: an unpainted fence becomes a painted fence meeting the required standard.

• Worldview: amateur painting can improve the property's appearance.

• Environmental constraint: hand painting is treated as a given restriction in this example.

Information and Library Services

An Imperial Chemical Industries (ICI) information and library services division explored its future while staffing fell from 32 to 25. Its activities included library services, chemical samples, safety reports and databases. Alternative definitions emphasised supporting wealth-creating business, providing comprehensive information, or meeting the needs of particular critical users. The breadth of existing activities did not determine a single purpose.

A Bridge from Three Perspectives

Perspective

Transformation

Purpose or evaluative emphasis

Government

Public funds become a community bridge

Public service and political legitimacy

Project manager

Resources become a completed bridge

Cost, time and quality

Construction team

Assigned tasks become daily progress

Work completion and safety

The project manager coordinates delivery but does not automatically hold the authority to stop the wider system.

Leave Approval

In an online leave-approval system, employees are customers, information technology and human resources staff are actors, and paper-based processing becomes online processing. The worldview values reduced processing time and efficiency. The human resources manager is the owner, while policies, system integration and time are constraints.

Education and Competing Purposes

A 10% fall over five years in the number of secondary-school students progressing to university does not itself establish what the school should do. Alternative purposes include preparation for university, employment or citizenship. A performance indicator cannot select the purpose without a value judgement.

Policing and Intervention Boundaries

An inquiry into policing activities associated with vice may involve parliament, courts, police, the public, providers, purchasers, social services, hospitals and residents. Intervention analysis makes visible whose concerns define the situation and who participates in interpreting it.

Concorde and Prisons

Concorde illustrates why engineering measures alone may not explain competing definitions of success. Alongside delays and cost overruns, the project had Anglo-French political purposes associated with Britain's attempt to join the European Community during a period of French opposition. Revealing additional purposes does not remove accountability for costs; it clarifies whose purposes inform evaluation.

A prison can be understood as a system for punishment, rehabilitation, deterrence, public protection or the unintended development of criminal capability. These are conceptual perspectives through which to investigate the institution, not necessarily mutually exclusive descriptions.

Cinema Perspectives

CATWOE element

Audience perspective

Commercial owner perspective

Worldview

Comfortable film viewing at a reasonable price

Film and related products generate returns for shareholders

Transformation

People seeking a film experience receive a comfortable viewing experience

Audience demand becomes sales of films, food, drinks and merchandise

Customers

Film viewers

Viewers and purchasers

Actors

Ticket sellers and projection staff

Operating roles may overlap with ownership roles

Owners

Shareholders

Ownership and some operating roles may overlap

Constraints

Film classification and health and safety

Film classification and food hygiene

The same owners can appear in different analyses while purposes, transformations and constraints receive different emphasis. Comparing perspectives can expose common ground and conflict without guaranteeing permanent agreement.

Parramatta Light Rail

A rich picture can include government, Transport for New South Wales, contractors, local businesses, commuters, residents and environmental groups. Relevant relationships include approvals, funding and feedback, as well as confusion, resistance and pride.

A local operational interpretation focuses on daily activity and the project team's role. A wider strategic interpretation focuses on city transformation, equity and accessibility. Comparing these interpretations demonstrates that a project has different meanings for different participants; neither interpretation alone exhausts the situation.

Practical Development of Soft Systems Thinking

Peter Checkland's movement from industrial management to systems research reflected the limitations of engineering approaches when applied to human and managerial situations. His central contribution was to use models to support learning between perspectives rather than assume a single fixed system awaiting optimisation. This approach connects management, information systems and education through inquiry directed toward action.
